claims.text: Premelting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by surface chemical segregation.
Lower-melting-point or lower-cohesion elements preferentially accumulate at the nanoparticle surface.
Enrichment of such elements lowers the effective local melting temperature at the surface.
The lowered surface melting temperature causes a premelting layer to form before the nanoparticle core melts.
The initial CoCrFeMnNi or AlCoCrFeNi nanoparticles are well alloyed and nearly compositionally uniform.
Controlled annealing can induce surface segregation without causing bulk phase separation.
Restricting particle sizes to 5–50 nm minimizes size effects in the comparison.
Segregation produces a surface compositional gradient and a thin, less-stable surface layer.
Surface segregation reduces the local cohesive energy at the nanoparticle exterior.
Reduced exterior cohesive energy causes local atomic mobility to begin earlier at the surface than in the core.
The resulting surface-first mobility controls the nanoparticle's overall thermal stability and melting behavior.
Surface-segregated nanoparticles will exhibit a detectable premelting layer at a lower temperature than uniformly mixed nanoparticles.
The extent of the premelting layer will increase as the degree of surface segregation increases.
The hypothesis applies when alloy mixing enthalpies permit moderate segregation.
Surface-to-volume effects relevant to the hypothesis are significant for particles typically smaller than 50 nm.
Support interactions, extreme particle sizes, or secondary phases may dominate or confound thermal behavior.
A DSC endothermic event can identify the onset of premelting.
In situ TEM can visualize a disordered or liquid-like premelting layer at the nanoparticle surface.
No significant difference in premelting onset or surface structure between segregated and uniform particles would falsify the proposed governing role of segregation.
